SearchQueryParam.name: q
SearchQueryParam.description:
Search query using field:value syntax. Multiple conditions separated by
spaces are ANDed together.

**URL Encoding:** This parameter must be URL-encoded when sent over HTTP.
Most HTTP clients handle this automatically. Examples in this documentation
show human-readable syntax for clarity.

## Syntax

| Pattern | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| `term` | Full-text exact match | `john` |
| `*term*` | Full-text contains | `*john*` |
| `term*` | Full-text starts with | `john*` |
| `*term` | Full-text ends with | `*smith` |
| `field:value` | Exact match on field | `status:approved` |
| `field:*value*` | Contains (case-insensitive) | `name:*john*` |
| `field:value*` | Starts with | `name:john*` |
| `field:*value` | Ends with | `email:*@example.com` |
| `field:"value"` | Quoted value (for spaces) | `name:"john doe"` |
| `field.nested:value` | Nested field (dot notation) | `address.state:CA` |
| `field:>value` | Greater than | `income:>1000` |
| `field:>=value` | Greater than or equal | `income:>=1000` |
| `field:<value` | Less than | `income:<5000` |
| `field:<=value` | Less than or equal | `income:<=5000` |
| `field:val1,val2` | Match any value (OR) | `status:approved,pending` |
| `-field:value` | Exclude / negate | `-status:denied` |
| `field:*` | Field exists (not null) | `email:*` |
| `-field:*` | Field does not exist | `-deletedAt:*` |

## Examples

- `john` — exact match for "john" in searchable fields
- `*john*` — contains "john" in searchable fields
- `name:*smith*` — name contains "smith" (case-insensitive)
- `email:*@example.com` — email ends with "@example.com"
- `status:approved` — exact match on status field
- `status:approved,pending` — status is "approved" OR "pending"
- `income:>=1000` — income greater than or equal to 1000
- `created:>2024-01-01` — created after January 1, 2024
- `status:approved income:>=1000` — approved AND income >= 1000 (multiple conditions)
- `-status:denied` — exclude records with status "denied"
- `-deletedAt:*` — only records where deletedAt does not exist
- `applicant.state:CA` — nested field filter

## URL Encoding Reference

When manually constructing URLs, encode these characters:

| Character | Encoded |
|-----------|---------|
| (space) | `%20` or `+` |
| `"` | `%22` |
| `:` | `%3A` |
| `>` | `%3E` |
| `<` | `%3C` |
| `,` | `%2C` |

**Example:**
```
Human-readable: q=status:approved income:>=1000
URL-encoded:    q=status%3Aapproved%20income%3A%3E%3D1000
```

SortParam.name: sort
SortParam.description:
Comma-separated list of fields to sort the response by. Prefix a field
with `-` for descending order. The first field is the primary sort;
subsequent fields are tie-breakers in declaration order.

**URL Encoding:** This parameter must be URL-encoded when sent over HTTP.
Most HTTP clients handle this automatically. Examples below show
human-readable syntax for clarity.

Which fields a given list endpoint allows is declared in the operation's
`x-sortable.fields` extension. Sending a field name not present in that
list returns `400 FIELD_NOT_SORTABLE`. Sending a field name that doesn't
exist on the resource schema returns `400 INVALID_SORT_FIELD`. When this
parameter is omitted, the operation's `x-sortable.default` (if declared)
is applied; otherwise no client-driven sort is applied. A configured
tie-breaker (default `id`) is always appended for stable pagination.

See `api-patterns.yaml#sorting` for the full convention and
`docs/architecture/x-extensions.md` for the extension shape.

## Syntax

| Pattern | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| `fieldName` | Ascending | `sort=createdAt` |
| `-fieldName` | Descending | `sort=-createdAt` |
| `field1,field2` | Multi-field | `sort=status,-priority` |
| `nested.field` | Nested field via dot notation | `sort=name.lastName` |

## Examples

- `sort=createdAt` — oldest first
- `sort=-createdAt` — newest first
- `sort=-priority,dueDate` — highest priority first, then oldest due date
- `sort=name.lastName,name.firstName` — alphabetical by surname, then given name

IdempotencyKeyParam.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKeyParam.description:
A key the client makes for one create, so a retry is not a second create.
Send the same key with every retry of the same request: the first is
created, and a repeat gets the same response back. The same key with a
different request is refused with 422. Keys are scoped to the caller.

Any value unique to the operation works; a UUID is recommended. An
operation that lists this parameter requires it. Follows the IETF HTTP API
working group's `Idempotency-Key` header draft, and the convention Stripe
and others use.

info.title: Transcripts
info.description:
The written record of a conversation. Starting a transcript opens it for
recording; pausing takes the conversation off the record; closing ends it.
A transcript refers to what it records — an interview, a call — and names
the profile it was started under, which says the transcription service,
and the client and model that produced its lines. Updating corrects what
it records; deleting removes it, and the event left behind says which one
and by whom.

A profile is a state's choice of transcription service and languages for
a kind of conversation. The deployment's config seeds them; they can be
added and changed here, never deleted, so every transcript's profile
still exists.

Its entries are its timeline, in the order things happened: lines, gaps
where nothing was captured, and pauses. Every time on a transcript and its
entries is the client's — when it started, paused, resumed and closed, and
when each line was said — so they are compared on one clock.

newest createdAt already read>`, skipping ids already read. `startedAt`
is the client's clock, so a line can arrive after one that started
later than it; `createdAt` still puts it after the last read.

interviewFlags.risks.earnedIncomeVaries.reason: Earned income is the largest source of payment errors, and wages that change month to month are the hardest to get right: a single pay stub doesn't show what a month of irregular hours or tips comes to.
probeQuestions: How many hours have you worked each week over the last month?
Do you get tips? About how much in a typical week?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.cashOrSelfEmploymen.reason: Cash, gig and self-employment income often isn't on the application at all, and isn't asked about unless someone asks specifically.
probeQuestions: Does anyone in the household do any work for cash, side jobs, or gig work?
About how much did that bring in over the last 30 days?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing

interviewFlags.risks.incomeChangedSinceP.reason: Income that's changed since the household on record — a job gained or lost, a raise, hours cut — is a leading cause of both overpayments and underpayments when it isn't reported. On a new application, that's since the application was filed.
probeQuestions: Has anyone started or stopped a job since your last renewal?
Has anyone's pay or hours changed?

sources.title: FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing
FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)

interviewFlags.risks.householdChangedSin.reason: Who lives in the household and buys food together decides whose income counts. Changes are often unreported, and often not asked about at recertification.
probeQuestions: Has anyone moved in or out since your last renewal?
Does everyone who lives with you buy and prepare food together?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)

interviewFlags.risks.shelterCostsCarried.reason: Shelter costs carried forward from the last certification without being asked about can be out of date in either direction: a move or a rent increase that's missed.
probeQuestions: Is your rent or mortgage still the same amount?
Have you moved since your last renewal?

sources.title: FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.elderlyOrDisabledWi.reason: A member 60 or older, or disabled, may deduct medical costs. Missed deductions are among the most common fixable errors, and lead to underpayments.
probeQuestions: Does [member] pay for any doctor visits, prescriptions, or medical supplies?
About how much a month?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates
FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing

interviewFlags.risks.childrenAndEarnersW.reason: Care for a child so a household member can work is deductible. When it's new it often isn't asked about, which leads to an underpayment.
probeQuestions: Does anyone look after the children while you work or go to school?
Do you pay for that care?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.multipleProgramsApp.reason: Households on several programs face reporting rules that differ between them, which makes it harder to keep each program's information right.
probeQuestions: Have you reported this change to [other program] as well?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.incomeBel.reason: When reported income doesn't cover reported expenses, something the application doesn't show is paying the difference: unreported income, or help from outside the household. FNS-1104 makes it a probe.
probeQuestions: Your expenses are more than your income. How does the household make up the difference?
Does anyone help with bills — family, friends, or community organizations?

sources.title: FNS State SNAP Interview Toolkit (FNS-1104, revised June 2025)

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.wagesDiff.reason: Income an agency's data systems show but nobody confirms is an error the agency could have caught. A difference from the wage records needs explaining before it's resolved either way.
probeQuestions: The state's records show [amount] in wages for [member]. Does that sound right?
Did [member] have another job, or more hours, during that time?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.incomeDif.reason: A recorded amount that doesn't match its pay stubs usually means a pay frequency was converted wrongly — weekly, every two weeks, and twice a month are easy to confuse.
probeQuestions: How often is [member] paid — every week, every two weeks, or twice a month?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.household.reason: The household's size decides its benefit. A size that doesn't match the members listed means someone is missing or counted who shouldn't be.
probeQuestions: Who lives with you and buys and prepares food with you?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.jobWithou.reason: A job with no income recorded is information that arrived but wasn't applied — the most common kind of agency error.
probeQuestions: Is [member] still working at [job]? How much are they paid?

sources.title: APHSA: Payment Error Rates — Understanding What They Are and How to Support SNAP Agencies in Reducing Them

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.earnedInc.reason: Earned income with no job behind it can't be verified or updated when the job changes, and is often a job that ended but wasn't closed out.
probeQuestions: Where does [member] work? Are they still working there?

sources.title: APHSA: Payment Error Rates — Understanding What They Are and How to Support SNAP Agencies in Reducing Them

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.utilities.reason: A household that pays a utility bill isn't one whose utilities are all included in the rent, and which it is decides whether a utility allowance applies. What counts as a utility deduction is a common misapplication of policy.
probeQuestions: Do you pay any utility bills yourself, like electric or gas, or are they all included in the rent?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

    .map(i, i.amount * monthlyFactor[i.frequency]).sum() >= v.amount / 3.0 * (1.0 - constants.differenceAllowed)

info.title: The application walk-through
info.description:
A household applies for SNAP online and a caseworker takes the application from submission to close, showing what the mock does from the contracts alone:

- separate shapes for what a client writes and what the system keeps, and derived fields
- a file upload and an expanded relationship
- search, sorting and paging
- a lifecycle that refuses moves made out of turn
- a composed view, and rules that explain their answers
- one event log across every domain
- the mock's own stand-ins and reset

workflows.summary: An application from creation to close, through every kind of thing the contracts declare.

steps.description:
Create an application

- You sent an `ApplicationCreate` and got back an `Application` — two schemas, not one. The contract declares the shape a client may write separately from the shape the system keeps.
- `id`, `confirmationNumber`, `status`, `submittedAt`, `openedAt` are marked `readOnly`, so they are not on the shape you sent at all. The server filled them in because the contract says they exist.
- `programCount` is declared as a derived field, with the expression `this.programsAppliedFor.size()`. Nothing stores it: the mock evaluates that expression every time the record is read.
- `channel` is an enum in the contract — `online`, `phone`, `in_person`, `mail`. A value outside that list is refused by the schema, and no validation was written for this endpoint to do it.
- `201` and `400`, `422`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the mock worked out which one applied and returned it. None of them are canned.

Upload a document

- This body is `multipart/form-data`, not JSON. The contract declares `file` with `format: binary`, which is how an OpenAPI document says bytes, and `documentTypeId`, `title` alongside it as ordinary fields. One operation in the whole set sends something that is not JSON, and it is the one most mocks fall over on.
- What came back describes the upload and does not contain it. The bytes were hashed as they were read and then dropped — `contentHash` and `sizeBytes` are kept on the version this created, which `latestVersionId` names, and the file itself is nowhere. Nothing the mock holds can leak something nobody meant to share.

file.content: Hashed on the way in, and then thrown away.

steps.description:
Attach a document that isn't there

- Refused with `422`. `proofOfIncomeDocumentId` declares `x-relationship` to document management's `Document`, so the mock looked for that document and found none.
- The refusal names the field and the id, in the same shape as a schema error. The id is a valid uuid, so the schema had nothing to object to.
- The check crosses domains, from intake into document management, and nothing was written for it. Every field that declares a relationship is checked the same way, on every create and update.

Edit and attach the document

- A third shape: `ApplicationUpdate` is what you may send here, and it is not `Application` either.
- `proofOfIncomeDocumentId` is the id of the `Document` you uploaded a moment ago, and `proofOfIncomeDocument` is the whole record. The document-management domain declares that shape, this one declares a relationship to it, and the mock put what the id points at where the id was — one request rather than two, and nothing joining them in a client.
- `updatedAt` moved on its own. Everything the request did not mention is as it was.
- `id`, `confirmationNumber`, `status` are not on `ApplicationUpdate` at all, so there is no way to send them and nothing to reject.
- `200` and `400`, `404`, `422`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the mock worked out which one applied and returned it. None of them are canned.

List the applications

- `q`, `sort`, `limit` are in the request above, and `q`, `limit`, `offset`, `sort`, `status`, `channel` are all declared on the operation. Declaring them was the whole of the work — the searching, filtering and paging came with them.
- `x-sortable` lists `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `submittedAt`, `status`, `channel` as the fields that may be sorted, and `-createdAt` as the order when a request does not say. Any other field is refused by name. The allowlist is that declaration — there is no check written for this endpoint.
- `items`, `total`, `limit`, `offset` — the page envelope is the contract's shape, not a convention the mock chose.

Stand in for the scheduler

- Nothing in the contract set implements a scheduler, and `submit` asks for one `72 hours` out. That gap is declared, not accidental.
- This registers a stand-in for `scheduling.timer.requested`, so the callback lands the moment it is asked for. The contract did not change — the thing on the other end of it did.

Submit the application

- The contract declares this move as `draft → submitted`. From any other state the mock refuses it — not from a check somebody wrote for this endpoint, but by reading that line.
- This action also calls `requestTimer` with a `fireAfter` of 72 hours, which emits `scheduling.timer.requested`. The stand-in you registered answers it immediately, so `intake.review_reminder` is already in the event log rather than three days away.
- `slaTypeCode` and `slaInfo` are filled from an SLA contract: `snap_standard` runs 30 days, warns at 80% of it, and stops while `status` is `withdrawn`. The clock is a declaration, not a cron job somebody remembered to write.
- `submittedAt` is annotated with `snap-processing-clock`, which the shared policy registry resolves to 7 CFR § 273.2(g). SNAP application processing standards — 30-day processing clock from date of filing; expedited service within 7 days for qualifying households.
- `200` and `400`, `404`, `409`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the mock worked out which one applied and returned it. A `409` is declared here because the contract anticipates this call being made out of turn.

Close it from the wrong state

- The contract declares this move as `under_review → closed`, and the record is not in that state yet. Nothing checked for this case on purpose — the mock reads that line and answers from it, the same line the moves that worked read.
- Every lifecycle in the set is enforced this way, so a state machine nobody implemented is still a state machine you cannot get around.

Open the application

- `openedAt` was null until now. The lifecycle declares `set: openedAt = $now` on this move, so the field is written because the state machine says so — there is no handler here that writes it.

Close the application

- This move emits `intake.application.closed`, which the log a few steps on will have in it. Nothing subscribed to it and nothing called a publisher: the action declares an `emit` and the mock does it.

Build a view of the application

- Nothing stores this shape. The composition names `programsAppliedFor`, `status` and the mock reads those fields off the stored application when you ask for it.
- It also pulls in `members`, which live in their own collection. Reading this without the composition means a request for the application and 1 more for the rest, then assembling them in the client.
- This is where the `_links` on the application came from. `applicationSummary`, `applicationReview` set `parentLink`, so the mock added `/summary`, `/review` to every application it returns. The application's own schema says nothing about either of them.

Evaluate expeditedSnap

- The answer is not one expression but a chain of named facts. The last is `isExpeditedEligible = (isLowIncome && hasLowResources) || isCombinedUnderShelter || isMigrantWithLowResources` — so the system can say which condition carried, not just what it concluded.
- `incomeThreshold` is an input with a default of `150`, citing 7 CFR § 273.2(i)(1)(i). It is a number Congress changes, so the contract treats it as one rather than burying it in code.
- `resourceThreshold` is an input with a default of `100`, citing 7 CFR § 273.2(i)(1)(i). It is a number Congress changes, so the contract treats it as one rather than burying it in code.
- Every fact comes back as a `state` and a `value` rather than a bare answer. `complete` means everything it needed was given to it; a fact that fell back to a declared default says `placeholder` instead, so a caller can tell a real conclusion from a provisional one.

Gather what the interview flags compare against

- A renewal: a household already on SNAP recertifying.
- `previous` is the household as last certified, copied onto the renewal when it opened, so the baseline holds still through the review. `verified` is what the state's wage records and a verified pay stub show. `asOf` is the interview date.
- The `interviewFlagsInputs` composition translates the data model into the ruleset's inputs by alias — `interviewDate as asOf`, `previousHousehold as previous` — so the rules speak their own vocabulary and nothing between them maps by hand.

Evaluate interviewFlags

- `current` is what the household is reporting in the interview, sent by the worker's screen: the client's mother has moved in with Social Security, warehouse hours were cut, there's cash work cleaning offices, rent went up, and the electric bill is in the client's name. Everything else came from the step before.
- One call answers in two groups: `risks`, situations where payment errors are common, and `inconsistencies`, things in this case that don't agree. `risks.householdChangedSincePrevious` is true — the mother is new — and so is `inconsistencies.wagesDifferFromWageRecords`: the wage records show about 1800 a month, and the household reports about 1100.
- Every flag is worked out from data, never a conclusion the caller sent: ages from dates of birth and the interview date, monthly amounts from what's paid and how often.
- `interviewFlags.risks.elderlyOrDisabledWithoutMedicalCosts` carries more than a true or false. Its annotations give the reason, the questions to probe with, the regulation behind it (`snap-elderly-disabled-deductions`) and the sources the situation comes from.

See what the walk emitted

- Every change you made emitted one of these, and nothing asked for them. Uploading a document wrote to this log; so did submitting, opening and closing.
- The types are declared as channels in the contract set — `communication.transcript.created`, `communication.transcript.updated`, `communication.transcript.deleted`, `communication.transcript_entry.created`, and the rest.
- One log, every domain. Nothing wired them together.

Narrow the log to one record

- `q` is full text over the whole log, narrowed here to the application you created. The document upload drops out — it happened, but to a different subject.
- What is left was written by more than one domain. Submitting the application is what made eligibility start a determination, and neither domain was wired to the other: each declares its own channel, and this log is all they share.
- `sort` works here for the same reason it worked on the applications — this operation declares its own `x-sortable`, over `time`, `type`, `source`. Nothing was written twice to make both endpoints sortable.

Empty the store

- No contract declares this endpoint. It belongs to the mock, not to the system it is running.
- It clears records, never contracts — afterwards the API is exactly the API it was.

Put the data back

- The records come from the contract set's own `*-mock-data.yaml`, and are checked against the same schemas as anything you send.

info.title: A transcript, from start to close
info.description:
A caseworker's interview software transcribes an interview from start to close, then abandons a second transcript, exercising the transcription domain end to end:

- profiles, and what a transcript needs before it can start
- a timeline of lines, gaps and pauses, each judged by when it started
- retries recognized by their Idempotency-Key, and entries that never change
- closing, and the idle timeout, with the mock standing in for the scheduler

workflows.summary: Start, record, pause, resume and close a transcript, and see what it refuses.

steps.description:
Add a profile

- You sent a `TranscriptionProfileCreate` and got back a `TranscriptionProfile`: the shape an administrator writes, and the shape the system keeps.
- `provider` takes its values from the `transcription-services` registry, through `x-enum-source`. `aws-transcribe` is an entry there; a service no entry names is refused, and a contract set adds one with a registry file of its own.
- `source` is `user` for a profile added through the API, and `system` for the ones the config seeds.
- No `idleTimeout`, so transcripts under this profile never close for being idle.

Start without a model

- Refused with `409` by `modelGivenForTheService`: under a profile whose `provider` is a transcription service, a transcript has to say which `model` produced its lines.
- The refusal is the guard's description, written as a sentence. `profileExists` passed, so only the condition not met is named.
- A guard runs on a plain create because the state machine governs `Transcript` under `resources:`. No action is involved.

Start under a profile that does not exist

- Refused with `409` by `profileExists`: the guard reads the profile `profileId` names, through the machine's context, and there isn't one.
- Both guards run, and each one not met is named. `modelGivenForTheService` passes here, since without a profile there is no service to need a model.

Start the transcript

- `TranscriptCreate` requires `profileId`, `client` and `startedAt`. `model` is required by the guard, not the schema, because a profile whose `provider` is `none` needs none.
- `status` is `recording` because that is the state machine's initial state. Nothing in the request set it.
- `startedAt` is by the software's clock, and every time on the transcript's entries is compared on that same clock.

Add the first line

- `Idempotency-Key` is declared on this operation, from the shared parameters every domain uses. The mock remembers the key with its answer.
- The body is a `TranscriptLineCreate`, one of the kinds `TranscriptEntryCreate` chooses between by `kind`.
- `startedWhileRecording`, `endsAfterItStarts` and `gapOutsidePauses` all passed: the guards the machine puts on every new entry.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description:
Send it again

- Same `Idempotency-Key`, same body: the mock answers with the line it already stored, with the same `id` and `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. No second line is written.
- The same key with a different body would be refused with `422`. A retry is the same request; a new request needs a new key.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description:
Go off the record

- `pause` is an action of the transcript's state machine, from `recording` to `paused`, guarded by `atAfterStart`.
- Its steps write a `pause` entry with no `endedAt`, and emit `paused`, which resolve names `communication.transcript.paused`.
- `at` is by the software's clock too. `AtRequest` declares it, for pausing, resuming and closing alike.

A line said just before the pause

- It arrived after the pause, but its `startedAt` is before it, and `startedWhileRecording` judges an entry by when it started. Kept.
- Software sends a line once it is finished, so a line still being spoken when the pause came always arrives late.

payload.text: My two kids and my mother.
payload.speaker: client

steps.description:
A line said during the pause

- Refused with `409` by `startedWhileRecording`: a pause was open when the line started.
- The server refuses it, not the software. Nothing said off the record is kept, even from software that keeps sending.

A lost stretch overlapping the pause

- Refused with `409` by `gapOutsidePauses`. A gap is time the software lost, and the pause already accounts for that stretch.
- `cause` says why the time was lost: `connection` here, one of the values `GapCause` declares.

Back on the record

- `resume` goes from `paused` to `recording`, guarded by `aPauseIsOpen` and `atAfterPauseBegan`.
- It gives the open pause its `endedAt` with a `PATCH` the machine makes itself, then calls `requestIdleCheck`, which does nothing here: this profile has no `idleTimeout`.

A late line from inside the past pause

- Still refused by `startedWhileRecording`: the pause is over, but the line started inside it.

Read the timeline

- A `TranscriptEntryList`: lines, gaps and pauses together, in the order they happened by `startedAt`.
- `total` is 3: the two lines kept, and the pause with the `endedAt` resuming gave it. The refused entries left nothing behind.

Try to change an entry

- Refused with `403`: the machine lets only `system` update a `TranscriptEntry`, and the caller's role is checked before the body is.
- Resuming and closing end a pause through the machine's own steps, which are not held to this.

Close the transcript

- `close` goes from `recording` or `paused` to `closed`, and sets `closedAt` to the `at` sent.
- `lastActivityAt` is when the last line or gap ended, kept up to date by the machine's subscription to `communication.transcript_entry.created`. A pause doesn't count: it is the transcript's own entry, not the software's.

A line after the close

- Refused with `409` by `startedWhileRecording`: the line started after `closedAt`.

Add a profile with an idle timeout

- `idleTimeout` is an ISO 8601 duration, `PT30M`. A recording transcript under this profile that hears nothing for that long closes itself.

Stand in for the scheduler

- `requestIdleCheck` emits `scheduling.timer.requested`, asking the scheduler to send an `idle_check` once the profile's `idleTimeout` has passed.
- Nobody waits 30 minutes in a test. This stub, on the mock's own route, answers the next idle check request at once, as if the time had passed.

Start a transcript and go quiet

- Creating it asks for the first idle check: the machine's subscription to `communication.transcript.created` calls `requestIdleCheck`.
- No line or gap ever arrives.

It closed itself

- When the `idle_check` came, nothing had arrived since it was asked for, so the machine closed the transcript.
- It closed at `lastActivityAt`, or at `startedAt` when there was none, as here. An idle transcript closes when it was last heard from, not when the check ran.
